summary: Bronx light at the East River entrance: first lit in the 1820s, moved onto Fort Schuyler in 1906, discontinued in 1934. Keepers from 1826; the site is now on the SUNY Maritime campus.

lens.note: Fourth-order lens in the 1906 brick tower (LighthouseFriends; USLHS). Which lens the Maritime Industry Museum holds is not stated.

structures.note: First light; the archive gives 1827 as established and LighthouseFriends gives completion in 1826. Torn down in 1835.
Forty-foot temporary tower set up near Fort Schuyler (LighthouseFriends).
35 feet, built atop the walls of Fort Schuyler (LighthouseFriends; USLHS).
Sixty feet tall with a fixed red light (LighthouseFriends).
Plain modern tower displaying a red light (LighthouseFriends).

staffing.note: The archive lists keepers through the 1950s; the last entry is 'at least 1950-1959'.

access.note: Archive: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: grounds open, dwelling closed. The site lies on the SUNY Maritime College campus.

visit.note: LighthouseFriends reports the grounds open and the dwelling closed. Check with the college before visiting.

facts.agency: State University of New York Maritime College (owner of the dwelling, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: First lighthouse completed (LighthouseFriends). The archive gives 1827 as the year established.
First light and original keeper's dwelling torn down during the building of Fort Schuyler; a temporary forty-foot wooden octagonal tower set up near the fort (LighthouseFriends).
First fog bell established at the station (LighthouseFriends).
Fresnel lens replaced the old array of reflectors and lamps (LighthouseFriends).
Iron skeleton tower replaced the wooden tower (LighthouseFriends).
Oil house built at the station (Light-House Board report, fiscal year ended 30 June 1896).
War Department authorised to extend a battery embankment about six feet into the light-house reservation (Light-House Board report, fiscal year ended 30 June 1899).

Board recommends a small light on the bastion of Fort Schuyler, removal of the present light to storage, and other works; new tower estimated at $6,000 (Light-House Board report, fiscal year ended 30 June 1901).
Conical brick tower built atop the fort's walls replaced the iron tower; began operating 25 July 1906 with a fourth-order lens (LighthouseFriends; USLHS).
Charles A. Ferreira rescued a soldier whose canoe capsized off Fort Schuyler on 8 December 1929 (LighthouseFriends).
Station discontinued (USLHS). LighthouseFriends says the brick tower was discontinued that year and replaced by a skeletal tower.
Sixty-foot skeletal tower with a fixed red light, range eleven miles, replaced the brick tower (LighthouseFriends).
Adam L. Kohlman listed as principal keeper from 1944 (USLHS).
1934 tower replaced by a plain modern tower displaying a red light (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.why: The record's tower entry is brick, which matches the 1906 tower, not the 1827 first light. The archive gives the tower's year as 1906 and LighthouseFriends dates the conical brick tower to 1906.
The archive gives the brick tower as 35 feet from base to lantern centre, and LighthouseFriends gives a thirty-five-foot tower. 35 feet is about 10.7 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1934 Wikidata date belongs to the skeletal tower LighthouseFriends describes, which replaced the brick tower in 1934. The station's first light is the archive's 1827 date; LighthouseFriends gives 1826 for completion of the first lighthouse. The two early dates differ by a year, and the story states both.

notes_for_editor: Roster: the archive lists 22 lines, every one as Principal Lighthouse Keeper, normalised here to head keeper. Riley Sherwood appears twice. Lawrence Lewis (1857 to 1859) is named by LighthouseFriends only, between Sherwood and Kelly where the archive has a gap; kept with the LighthouseFriends citation and no person slug. Albert G. Possell is marked to_approx because the archive says 'at least 1950-1959'. Person slugs are the archive's, from roster.py --json. First light: the archive says 1827 established; LighthouseFriends says the first lighthouse was completed in 1826 and that the land was obtained in 1823 and building began in 1826 under the Daboll brothers. The Daboll names, the 1835 temporary tower, the 1838 leaky report, the 1854 fog bell, the 1855 lens, the 1890 tower, the 1906 contract and operation dates, the 1929 rescue, the 1944 ceremony and the bar anecdote all come from LighthouseFriends alone; the story attributes each to it. The Light-House Board's 1896 and 1899 entries are in the fiscal-year reports whose headings the local text shows; their printed page numbers were not confirmed, so the footnotes give scan pages. The 1901 entry is at printed p. 72, read from the running head before it (scan page 98). The 1901 estimate table is OCR'd; only the tower line ($6,000) is used and the total is not. Status is contested: the archive lists the station discontinued in 1934, 'Active Aid to Navigation? No', and 'House Remains, Tower Does Not'; LighthouseFriends describes a 1986 modern tower that displays a red light. The Wikidata record says active and the USLHS record says inactive; the question of whether a light still shows needs a Coast Guard Light List check and an on-site check. Focal height: the archive says 69 feet above mean high water (21.0 m) and the record says 18.3 m (ENC); range: LighthouseFriends says eleven miles for the 1934 tower (about 9.6 nautical miles), the record says 9.0 nautical miles (ENC). Neither is reconciled; the story gives the LighthouseFriends range only. The lens in the Maritime Industry Museum is not identified as the fourth-order lens. Wikipedia was read as a lead only and is not cited; its infobox gives 1906 as first lit, which conflicts with the archive. The USCG Historian's page for Throgs Neck could not be read: the archived copies returned only a wrapper, so it is not cited. Chronicling America: eight searches for New York papers, 1880 to 1935, on Throgs Neck with lighthouse and keeper terms, Ellen Lyons and Ferreira, and one page read, returned no usable item for the keepers, the 1906 tower, the 1934 change or the 1929 rescue. The 1929 rescue and the 1944 ceremony rest on LighthouseFriends, which cites The New York Sun of 9 August 1944 among its references; that article was not reached. The Board's annual reports in the local corpus mention Throgs Neck in the 1891 to 1901 lists of lights and in the three entries cited; the general histories in the corpus do not mention it.
